hints: Think about what hot concentrated acidified KMnO4 does to a C=C bond in a ring, the ring is cut open at the double bond and each C of the C=C becomes a C=O group.
walkthrough:
Picture M being cut open**
M is 1-methylcyclopent-1-ene, a five membered ring with a $\text{C=C}$ bearing a methyl group. Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ is a very vigorous oxidiser, it does not just add OH groups, it completely cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ bond.

Decide what each alkene carbon becomes**
One alkene carbon has one alkyl group plus the methyl group, so it is $\text{R}_{2}\text{C=}$. On cleavage it becomes a ketone, $\text{R-CO-CH}_{3}$. The other alkene carbon has one H and one alkyl group, $\text{RCH=}$, on vigorous cleavage it is oxidised all the way to a carboxylic acid, $\text{R-COOH}$. Opening the ring gives one straight chain containing both groups: $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}$, formula $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$.
Final answer: N is $\text{HOOCCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCH}_{3}$ (5-oxohexanoic acid, a keto-carboxylic acid).

hints: Compare the formulae of N, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$, and 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{3}$, and work out how many H atoms must be added, remembering NaBH4 reduces ketone but not carboxylic acid.
walkthrough:
Spot what is reduced and what is untouched**
$\text{NaBH}_{4}$ is a gentle reducing agent. It reduces the ketone $\text{C=O}$ in N to a secondary alcohol $\text{CH-OH}$, but it leaves the carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$ unchanged. So the carbon skeleton and oxygen count stay the same, only hydrogen is added.

Balance with [H]**
N is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3}$ and the product is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{3}$. The difference is 2 H atoms, which come from the reducing agent: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_{3} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{3}$$

hints: Visualise the shape around the ketone C=O carbon in N just before the hydride attacks, is it flat or tetrahedral?
Think about what happens when a flat group is attacked with equal probability from above and below the plane, what type of stereoisomers result at the new chiral centre?
walkthrough:
See the flat target**
The ketone carbon in N is $\text{sp}^{2}$ hybridised, trigonal planar. The $\text{C=O}$ and the two groups attached to it all lie in one plane. The incoming hydride nucleophile from $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ can therefore approach from above the plane or from below the plane with exactly the same chance.

Link equal attack to two products**
Attack from one side gives one configuration at the new $\text{CH(OH)}$ chiral centre, attack from the other side gives the mirror image configuration. Both enantiomers form in equal amounts, so you get a mixture of two optical isomers, a racemate, not a single compound.

Final answer: The ketone C=O group in N is planar and can be attacked from either side with equal probability.
This forms equal amounts of the two optical isomers / enantiomers of 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid, a racemic mixture.

hints: Use equation 1 as a model, the OH and COOH in the same molecule join to form COO in a ring plus H2O, count how many atoms will be in the new ring from 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid.
walkthrough:
Fold the molecule to join the ends**
5-hydroxyhexanoic acid has $\text{COOH}$ at C1 and $\text{OH}$ at C5. Just like in equation 1, the $\text{OH}$ attacks the carboxylic acid carbon, eliminating $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and forming an ester link $\text{COO}$ inside the same molecule.

Check the ring size**
Counting the carbonyl C plus the four chain carbons plus the O from the alcohol gives a six membered ring containing $\text{C(=O)-O}$. With the methyl substituent on the carbon attached to the ring oxygen, this is 6-methyl-tetrahydropyran-2-one.
Final answer: P is the six-membered lactone 6-methyl-tetrahydropyran-2-one, a cyclic ester formed by intramolecular esterification with loss of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: List the key bonds present in both N and 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid, for example C=O, O-H, C-O and C-H.
Look at Table 5.1 for the C=O region, compare carbonyl (ketone) 1670-1740 with carboxyl 1670-1740 and think whether the two spectra would show clearly separated peaks.
walkthrough:
Compare the functional groups side by side**
N has a ketone $\text{C=O}$ plus a carboxylic acid ($\text{C=O}$, $\text{C-O}$, $\text{O-H}$). The product has an alcohol ($\text{C-O}$, $\text{O-H}$) plus the same carboxylic acid. So almost every bond type appears in both molecules.

Use the table to see the overlap**
Table 5.1 shows carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and carboxyl $\text{C=O}$ at the same 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, ester is only just higher at 1710-1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. $\text{C-O}$ is broad at 1040-1300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ in both, and $\text{O-H}$ ranges also overlap. Because the absorptions fall in the same wavenumber ranges, the spectra look essentially the same and progress is hard to follow.

Final answer: Absorptions overlap / are very similar and indistinguishable.
Both molecules contain bonds in similar environments, e.g. both contain $\text{C=O}$, $\text{C-O}$, $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{C-H}$, with $\text{C=O}$ (ketone and carboxyl) absorbing in the same 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ region.

hints: Recall that the M+1 peak is mainly due to 13C, each carbon contributes about 1.1% relative to M+, so set up (M+1 abundance / M+ abundance) x (100 / 1.1) to find the number of carbons.
Once you know the number of carbons, use M+ = 72 to work out the rest of the formula and remember Q must be a cyclic ester, so try the smallest lactone that fits.
walkthrough:
Calculate the carbon count from the isotope peak**
The small M+1 peak at $m/e = 73$ is almost entirely due to molecules containing one $^{13}\text{C}$ atom. Each carbon adds about 1.1% to the M+1 intensity: $$\text{number of C} = \frac{\text{abundance M+1}}{\text{abundance M+}} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = \frac{3.15}{95.5} \times \frac{100}{1.1} \approx 3.0$$ So Q contains 3 carbon atoms.

Fit the mass and the functional group**
$M+$ is 72, so $M_{r} = 72$. Three carbons account for 36, leaving $72 - 36 = 36$. A lactone must contain two oxygens in the $\text{COO}$ group ($2 \times 16 = 32$), leaving 4 for hydrogens. That gives $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{2}$. The only cyclic ester with this formula is the four membered lactone oxetan-2-one.

Final answer: Number of C atoms = $\frac{3.15}{95.5} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 3$.
Q is oxetan-2-one, the four-membered cyclic ester $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{2}$ ($M_{r} = 72$).
